---
title: "Figure 2.1: Financial Conditions Index"
---

![Python: `python/fig-2-1.py`](../images/python/fig-2-1.png)

Quarterly financial conditions indices for LA5, the United States and
Canada. The index summarises many financial variables, such as interest
rates, spreads, exchange rates and equity prices, into one number. Positive
values mean tight conditions and negative values loose ones, so zero, the
neutral level, is the key reference line.

**New in this chart:**

- the x-axis line at zero, with tick marks;
- y-labels with one decimal.

This page explains the axis line at zero in detail. Many later charts
([3.1](fig-3-1.qmd), [3.3](fig-3-3.qmd), [5.2](fig-5-2.qmd),
[10.2](fig-10-2.qmd)) use the same technique.

## The data

Sheet `data`, 10 rows:

| category | LA5 | United States | Canada |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2024Q1 | 0.28 | -0.85 | 0.05 |

The quarters are text, so they are plotted at positions 0, 1, 2, .... The
values are small, between about -1 and 0.5, which is why the y-labels need a
decimal.

## The script

### Colours and frame

```python
series_colours = {
    "LA5": "#5B267A",
    "United States": "#0066A6",
    "Canada": "#404040",
}
```

The usual REO colours: purple for the Latin American aggregate, blue for
the United States, dark grey for Canada.

The subtitle, `"(0 = neutral; +/– = tight/loose)"`, contains an en dash
(`–`), not a hyphen. Python strings can hold any character, so it is typed
as it appears in the published chart. `bottom_gap=0.62` leaves room for the
vertical quarter labels.

### The axis line at zero

```python
x = np.arange(len(data))

# The x-axis is drawn at zero, with short tick marks pointing up.
ax.axhline(0, color="black", linewidth=0.9)
ax.vlines(x, 0, 0.035, color="black", linewidth=0.7)
```

In the published chart, the horizontal axis crosses at zero, in the middle
of the plot, with its tick marks there, while the quarter labels are at the
bottom. In Excel this is the combination of *Vertical axis crosses at 0* and
*Label position: Low*.

matplotlib always draws the x-axis, with its ticks and labels, at the edge
of the plot. So the script splits the job:

- the **line** at zero is drawn with `ax.axhline(0, ...)`, which spans the
  full width of the plot;
- the **tick marks** are drawn with `ax.vlines(x, 0, 0.035, ...)`: one short
  vertical line at each quarter, from 0 up to 0.035;
- the **labels** stay on the normal x-axis at the bottom (see below).

The tick height (0.035) is in data units, not points. On this scale from -1
to 0.6, it is about 2 percent of the plot height, which gives a short tick.
If you change the y-range, check the tick height too: on a scale from -10 to
6, 0.035 would be invisible. See [An axis line at
zero](../techniques.qmd#sec-axis-line).

### The lines

```python
for series, colour in series_colours.items():
    ax.plot(x, data[series], color=colour, linewidth=1.8,
            solid_capstyle="butt", label=series)
```

`solid_capstyle="butt"` ends the lines exactly at the first and last point.
Most charts in this book use round ends, but here the x-axis starts and ends
exactly at the first and last quarter (see the limits below). A round end
extends half a line width beyond the point, so it would stick out past the
edge of the plot. See [Line styles](../techniques.qmd#sec-line-styles).

### The x-axis

```python
ax.set_xticks(x, data["category"], rotation=90)
ax.set_xlim(0, len(data) - 1)
ax.spines["bottom"].set_visible(False)
ax.tick_params(axis="x", length=0, pad=7)
```

- **The labels** are the quarter names, under each position, written
  vertically.
- **The limits** are exactly the first and last positions, 0 and 9, so the
  lines run from edge to edge.
- **The bottom spine is hidden.** A *spine* is matplotlib's name for the
  lines around the plot area. The house style already hides the top and
  right ones; here the bottom one goes too, because the axis line is now the
  one at zero.
- **No tick marks at the bottom** (`length=0`). The quarter labels remain,
  7 points below the bottom of the plot (`pad=7`).

### The y-axis

```python
ax.set_ylim(-1, 0.6)
ax.yaxis.set_major_locator(MultipleLocator(0.2))
ax.yaxis.set_major_formatter(FormatStrFormatter("%.1f"))
ax.tick_params(axis="y", length=2.8, pad=5)
```

The y-axis runs from -1 to 0.6 with a tick every 0.2. Zero is one of the
ticks, so the axis line at zero lines up with a label.

`FormatStrFormatter("%.1f")` writes every label with exactly one decimal:
-1.0, -0.8, ..., 0.6. `%.1f` means "a number with one digit after the
decimal point", like the Excel number format `0.0`. With a tick every 0.2,
matplotlib would choose one decimal anyway, but its automatic format depends
on the scale. Setting it makes sure the labels stay in the published format
whatever the data. See [Number formats](../techniques.qmd#sec-number-formats).

### The legend

```python
ax.legend(loc="center left", bbox_to_anchor=(0.05, 0.49),
          handlelength=2.9, labelspacing=0.15)
```

The legend is anchored by its left middle (`"center left"`): the middle of
its left edge is put at 5 percent from the left and 49 percent from the
bottom of the plot. That is slightly below the middle, in the gap between
the lines above and below zero. Anchoring by the centre rather than a corner
keeps the legend in that gap even if you add or remove an entry. See
[Legends](../techniques.qmd#sec-legends).

## Changing the chart

- **Ticks pointing down** instead of up, as in [Figure 3.3](fig-3-3.qmd):
  `ax.vlines(x, -0.035, 0, ...)`.
- **A wider y-range.** If new data go below -1, use for example
  `ax.set_ylim(-1.4, 0.6)`. Keep zero on a tick and adjust the tick height
  if the range grows a lot.
- **Round line ends.** If you add half a step of margin,
  `ax.set_xlim(-0.5, len(data) - 0.5)`, round ends no longer stick out and
  you can use `solid_capstyle="round"`.

## The complete script

The full `python/fig-2-1.py`, as it runs:

```` {.python filename="python/fig-2-1.py"}
"""Figure 2.1: Financial Conditions Index."""
import numpy as np
from matplotlib.ticker import FormatStrFormatter, MultipleLocator

from chart_style import new_chart, read_chart_data, save_chart

STEM = "fig-2-1"

data = read_chart_data(STEM)

series_colours = {
    "LA5": "#5B267A",
    "United States": "#0066A6",
    "Canada": "#404040",
}

fig, ax = new_chart(
    title="Financial Conditions Index",
    subtitle="(0 = neutral; +/– = tight/loose)",
    caption=(
        "Source: IMF staff calculations.\n"
        "Note: For methodology and variables included in the financial conditions\n"
        "index, refer to the online annex of the October 2018 Global Financial\n"
        "Stability Report. LA5 is purchasing-power-parity GDP-weighted averages.\n"
        "LA5 = Latin America 5 (Brazil, Chile, Colombia, Mexico, Peru)."
    ),
    left=0.4,
    right=0.15,
    bottom_gap=0.62,
)

x = np.arange(len(data))

# The x-axis is drawn at zero, with short tick marks pointing up.
ax.axhline(0, color="black", linewidth=0.9)
ax.vlines(x, 0, 0.035, color="black", linewidth=0.7)

for series, colour in series_colours.items():
    ax.plot(x, data[series], color=colour, linewidth=1.8,
            solid_capstyle="butt", label=series)

ax.set_xticks(x, data["category"], rotation=90)
ax.set_xlim(0, len(data) - 1)
ax.spines["bottom"].set_visible(False)
ax.tick_params(axis="x", length=0, pad=7)

ax.set_ylim(-1, 0.6)
ax.yaxis.set_major_locator(MultipleLocator(0.2))
ax.yaxis.set_major_formatter(FormatStrFormatter("%.1f"))
ax.tick_params(axis="y", length=2.8, pad=5)

ax.legend(loc="center left", bbox_to_anchor=(0.05, 0.49),
          handlelength=2.9, labelspacing=0.15)

save_chart(fig, STEM)
````
